extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ancient philosophy; readers of Platonic commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly commentary and interpretation of Plato's Republic (esp. Book IX) addressing the Platonic 'number' puzzle, the classification of pleasures, character-types (king/tyrant), and methods for reading Plato's numerical and ethical imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand Platonic numerical passages by close philological study
rubrics_metrics.description: Our hope of understanding the passage depends principally on an accurate study of the words themselves; on which a faint light is thrown by the parallel passage in the ninth book. Another help is the allusion in Aristotle, who makes the important remark that the latter part of the passage describes a solid figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close reading of the Greek wording, consult parallel Platonic passages, and use Aristotle's allusions as corroboration; bring in knowledge of ancient mathematics (e.g., Pythagorean triangle 3,4,5) to reconstruct Plato's meaning rather than assuming modern arithmetic. Examples: link terms like 'terms'/'intervals' to musical/arithmetical senses; consider geometrical figure references cited by Aristotle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume Plato intentionally used obscure expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: As little reason is there for supposing that Plato intentionally used obscure expressions; the obscurity arises from our want of familiarity with the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing deliberate deception or 'practising upon his readers' to Plato without strong evidence. First seek historical, mathematical, and linguistic explanations for obscurity before concluding intentional mystification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pythagorean numerology and ancient numeric traditions in interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s number-figures (e.g., 216, 8000, 5040, 729) are tied to Pythagorean ideas (3,4,5 triangle, tetractys) and ancient usages (e.g., 8000 as ancient number of Spartan citizens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a Platonic number appears, test hypotheses against Pythagorean motifs, sequences (tetractys), known ancient population numbers, and traditional associations (e.g., musical intervals, periods of metempsychosis). Use corroborating ancient testimony (Herodotus, Plutarch, Proclus, Quintilian) and check algebraic/figurative relations (squares, cubes) rather than imposing modern numeric intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate and render Greek mathematical/musical terms cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Words such as 'terms' (notes), 'intervals', 'base' (lowest term), and phrases rendered 'squared and cubed' or 'equalling and equalled in power' have multiple plausible translations and technical senses in number and music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare alternative translations (Donaldson, Weber, etc.), clarify whether a term refers to musical/arithmetical concepts, and be explicit about choices (e.g., 'by involution and evolution' vs 'squared and cubed'). Provide examples illustrating each translation's consequences for the reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Platonic numerical devices as symbolic/allegorical rather than strictly empirical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato uses arithmetic and geometrical figures as symbolic vehicles to express magnitude or relations (e.g., 729 expresses an 'interval' between king and tyrant and is presented as nearly equal to days and nights in the year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret such numbers as rhetorical/archetypal devices communicating relative magnitudes and philosophical points, not necessarily as literal empirical claims. Use the arithmetic to clarify Plato’s intended scale or metaphor, but avoid over-literalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify pleasures by soul-parts and judge their worth by reason and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures answer to the three elements of the soul—reason, passion, desire—and the pleasure of the rational part, based on truest knowledge and widest experience, is the truest pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the value of pleasures in Platonic terms, use the criterion of which part of the soul grasps truth and has experience (reason > ambition > money-making). Prefer pleasures tied to intellectual truth as more genuinely pleasurable; evaluate lives by their dominant principle’s access to knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pure pleasures from mere absence-of-pain and recognize pleasures without antecedent pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure pleasure is not simply the absence of pain; some pleasures (e.g., smell, hope, anticipation) have no antecedent pains and are not mere reliefs from pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing all pleasure to pain-relief in interpretation; identify pleasures that are direct positive states (anticipation, sensory pleasures) and treat their phenomenology and status differently when evaluating Plato's account of well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the soul–state analogy to evaluate political character and happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Like man, like State—the condition of an individual’s soul (freedom vs enslavement of reason) corresponds to the condition of a State; the tyrannical man/state is the most miserable and enslaved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political forms or individual characters, map internal psychic structure onto political structure: degree of rule by reason versus appetite indicates freedom and happiness; use this as a diagnostic for moral-political evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational and legal aim: cultivate self-control by strengthening the rational principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The law desires to nurse up in the young a higher principle (self-control); education should strengthen the 'man' (rational part) so that the many-headed appetites are controlled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Plato’s prescriptions for education and law as aiming to produce harmony by developing reason. In practical application, justify temporary regulation (e.g., placing handicraft arts under control) as a means to foster later self-mastery, not as permanent repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of bold numeric assignments without adequate proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators may assert correspondences (e.g., first/divine number = world, imperfect number = state, second harmony being a cube) without sufficient proof; such assignments require demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explicit argumentative support before accepting determinations that a Platonic number corresponds to a particular cosmic or civic period. Cross-check arithmetic identities, historical plausibility, and the textual contexts used to justify such claims (as with Donaldson and Schleiermacher debates).
